common_name: Kathleen Harrop Rose (Shell-Pink Thornless Climbing Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root plants in early spring against a pillar, fence, or wall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Kathleen Harrop is a shell-pink sport of the thornless climbing Bourbon rose Zephirine Drouhin, discovered and brought into commerce by the Dickson nursery in Northern Ireland. It carries the same nearly thornless, lax canes and strong old-rose fragrance as its parent, but opens a softer, more silvery pink that pales further as the semi-double blooms age. Train the long canes on a pillar, fence, or low wall, where it repeats reasonably well through the season and handles a bit more shade than most climbers. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape the plant and encourage continued rebloom.

common_name: Coupe d'Hebe Rose (Clear Pink Globular Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing room to train as a short climber if desired.

directions: Coupe d'Hebe is a nineteenth-century Bourbon rose valued for its very double, cupped flowers of clear, soft pink that open from rounded buds into a neat, almost rosette-like form. The strongly fragrant blooms appear in a heavy spring flush with a lighter repeat later in the season, carried on an upright, fairly vigorous shrub that can also be trained as a short climber against a support. Give it full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and remove old or crossing canes in late winter to keep growth open and productive. It is notably healthy and tolerates a bit more shade than many other Bourbons.

common_name: Belle Isis Rose (Pale Pink Myrrh-Scented Gallica Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Belle Isis is a French Gallica rose bearing flat, double, soft pink flowers noted for an unusual myrrh-like fragrance rather than the classic old-rose scent typical of most Gallicas. It flowers once, in a single abundant flush in late spring, on a compact, twiggy shrub that suckers modestly and tolerates poor soil better than most modern roses. Belle Isis is historically notable as a parent of the English shrub rose Constance Spry, which inherited some of its distinctive myrrh fragrance. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after the spring bloom, since Gallicas flower on wood formed the previous season.
sources: Graham Stuart Thomas, The Old Shrub Roses

common_name: Surpasse Tout Rose (Deep Cerise-Pink Double Gallica Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Surpasse Tout is an early French Gallica rose bearing very double, deep cerise-pink flowers that open flat and reflex attractively as they age, carrying the rich, classic fragrance typical of the class. Like other Gallicas, it blooms only once each year, in a dense, heavy flush in late spring, on a compact, upright, suckering shrub well suited to a mixed border or dedicated old-rose collection. It performs reliably in average, well-drained soil without heavy feeding, and tolerates poor soil and some neglect better than modern repeat-flowering roses. After the spring bloom finishes, remove only dead, damaged, or crossing canes, since next year's flowers form on this season's mature wood.

common_name: Marcel Bourgouin Rose (Velvety Wine-Purple Gallica Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Marcel Bourgouin is a French Gallica rose prized for unusually dark, velvety wine-purple to maroon double flowers that fade toward a soft slate-mauve as they age, giving the bush a shifting range of color through its bloom period. It flowers once, in a single rich flush in late spring, with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance, on a compact, upright shrub typical of the Gallica class. Grow it in full sun and average, well-drained soil, where it needs little feeding and tolerates poor conditions better than modern roses. Limit pruning to removing dead or crossing wood once flowering has finished, since the following year's bloom forms on this season's growth.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Alika is an old Gallica rose distinguished from most others in its class by large, single to semi-double cerise-red flowers with a prominent boss of golden stamens. It flowers once in late spring in a brief but showy display, followed by an abundant crop of glossy orange-red hips that persist into autumn and extend the plant's season of interest. Alika grows noticeably larger and more vigorous than typical compact Gallicas, forming a tall, arching shrub, and is valued by cold-climate gardeners for its unusually strong winter hardiness. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after flowering, since it blooms on the previous season's growth.
